prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the time-reversal-invariant topological insulator and quantum spin Hall effect, and the first experimental observation of the quantum spin Hall state

statement.case_for: B030 remains my first choice after reading the opening ballots. It is the textbook pattern of a Nobel-worthy discovery: a theoretical proposal (Kane and Mele's Z2 classification and quantum spin Hall effect in graphene) that created a new organising principle for quantum matter, followed by a clean experimental realisation in HgTe/CdTe quantum wells by Molenkamp's group. The idea has proven fertile well beyond its origin, in 3D topological insulators, topological photonics, superconductivity and quantum devices, and has been confirmed by many independent groups for nearly two decades. It is also the candidate that three members (Johansson, Pearce, and myself) put in their top three and that Mehlig ranks fourth, while Eriksson ranks a related topological-insulator ballot fourth, so there is broad agreement that the science is of the first rank.
statement.case_against: The 2016 prize to Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz already honoured topological phases and phase transitions, so a sceptic can say the committee has paid for topology once. The attribution is also genuinely hard: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang made the HgTe prediction that Molenkamp's experiment tested, Hasan's group led the 3D topological insulator observations, and the three-person limit leaves at least one real contributor out. Practical applications are still limited, so the case rests on conceptual impact rather than technology.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks B021 first, and for B030 proposes Kane, Molenkamp and Hasan, leaving out Mele, with the three-person limit making the choice among Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan and Zhang contentious.
responses.response: I agree the attribution is the weak point, but I would not drop Mele. The Z2 classification and the graphene quantum spin Hall proposal were joint Kane-Mele papers, and separating them would be hard to defend. Hasan's 3D work is important, but it is a second step after the quantum spin Hall prediction and observation; if the committee prefers to honour the 3D materials it should say so as a distinct achievement rather than substitute Hasan for Mele. I do share Mehlig's point that B021 is a strong rival, though I regard its microscopic interpretation as less settled.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B021 first as a theory-led discovery in which the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model predicted the magic angle and the 2018 experiments confirmed it, and sees B030 as a clean theory-to-experiment chain in a Kane-Molenkamp pair.
responses.response: The theory-to-experiment structure of B021 is as clean as that of B030, and I take that seriously; I ranked it third. Two things hold me back. The superconducting and correlated states in twisted bilayer graphene still lack an agreed mechanism, which is more open than the quantum spin Hall classification, and the 2018 discovery is much younger. On B030, a Kane-Molenkamp pair is tidy but omits Mele, whose role in the original proposal is equal to Kane's, so I prefer the trio.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED (B002) first and trapped ions (B006) second, as foundational quantum-information platforms with strong independent confirmation, and also puts B030 third as very mature and timely.
responses.response: I respect the quantum-information argument, but I do not think either is yet the strongest case. For B002 the committee would have to leave out Girvin from a four-person list, and the Nobel Prize in Physics 2025 for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits makes a closely related circuit prize look premature. For B006 the 2012 prize for control of single quantum systems already covers much of the experimental basis. B030, in contrast, has no earlier prize on this exact discovery, since 2016 addressed topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall effect, not time-reversal-invariant insulators. I welcome Johansson's support for B030 as a real basis for common ground.

responses.point: Pearce also ranks B030 first and sees it as one of the strongest cases, but flags that the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that guided the HgTe experiment is not among the credited names.
responses.response: This is the right caveat, and I raised it in my own opening. My view is that Kane and Mele's prediction came first and defined the field, while Molenkamp's group delivered the decisive observation, so the trio is defensible even though BHZ is missing from the credit list. I do not think the committee should hide that omission, and the citation should be worded to credit the proposal and the first observation rather than imply all of topological insulator physics.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks (B024) first as the clearest advance in measurement precision, a clean two-person pair in Katori and Ye with independent confirmation at the 10^-18 level.
responses.response: B024 is a clean and deserving case, and the two-name attribution is much simpler than ours. My reservation is one of weight: the clock is an exceptional instrument and a path to redefining the second, but the conceptual reach of topological band theory is wider. I would keep it as a strong candidate for a later year rather than prefer it now, and I would be open to hearing whether the committee thinks a precision-measurement prize deserves priority.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would accept leaving out Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang (who are not on the shortlist credit) and Hasan, or would prefer a different trio.
Whether the 2016 topology prize makes a second topological prize too close in time for some members.
Whether the open question of the superconducting mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene will be seen as disqualifying or merely as normal for a young field.
I rely on my own recollection of the history rather than independently verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My PhD supervisor David Gross, early mentor Hector Rubinstein and co-author Thomas Van Riet work in string theory and gravity, and none is a credited candidate on this shortlist.
